academicTask1.prompt: The graph below shows the percentage of commuters in the city of Carrowmere who used four different modes of transport to travel to work between 1995 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Main mode of transport to work in Carrowmere, 1995–2020

keyFeatures: The car was the most common way to commute throughout, but its share fell from a peak of 61% in 2000 to 38% in 2020
Cycling grew far more than any other mode, from 6% to 26%, overtaking the bus in 2015 and the train in 2020
Bus use peaked at 24% in 2005 and then declined to 15%, the lowest share of the four modes by 2020
Rail dipped to 12% in 2005 before recovering steadily to 21%
academicTask1.model:
The line graph compares the percentage of commuters in Carrowmere who travelled to work by car, bus, bicycle and train over a 25-year period from 1995.

Overall, the car remained the dominant mode of transport throughout, although its share declined considerably. By contrast, cycling and rail travel both became more popular, with cycling showing the most dramatic growth, while bus use fell.

In 1995, 58% of commuters drove to work, and this figure edged up to a peak of 61% five years later. From 2000 onwards, however, car use fell steadily, reaching 38% in 2020. The bus was the second most common choice at the start, used by 22% of commuters; after a slight dip, it peaked at 24% in 2005 and then slid to just 15% by 2020, the lowest share of the four.

Cycling, in contrast, was the least popular option for the first decade, at around 5–7%, but it then took off, overtaking the bus in 2015 and the train in 2020 to reach 26%. Rail use followed a similar but gentler pattern: after dipping to 12% in 2005, it recovered to 21% by the end of the period.

academicTask1.prompt: The chart below shows the number of students who began undergraduate courses in five subject areas in one country in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: New undergraduate students by subject area, 2005 and 2025

keyFeatures: Business was the most popular subject area in both years, but its lead over the second subject narrowed to just 3,000 students in 2025
Computing grew fastest, more than tripling from 21,000 to 68,000 and rising from the least popular area to the second most popular
Arts and humanities was the only area to decline, falling from 52,000 to 33,000 and becoming the least popular subject
Engineering and medicine and health both grew moderately (by 7,000 and 12,000 respectively)
academicTask1.model:
The bar chart compares the number of students, in thousands, who began undergraduate degrees in five subject areas in one country in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, enrolments rose in every field except arts and humanities, which saw a significant decline. The most striking change was the rapid growth of computing, which almost caught up with business, the most popular area in both years.

In 2005, business attracted 64,000 new students, followed by arts and humanities with 52,000. Engineering and medicine and health were less popular, with 38,000 and 29,000 entrants respectively, while computing was the smallest field at only 21,000.

Twenty years later, the picture had changed considerably. Computing enrolments had more than tripled to 68,000, just 3,000 below business, which had grown modestly to 71,000. Medicine and health recorded the second-largest increase, rising by 12,000 to 41,000, and engineering also grew, reaching 45,000. By contrast, the number of arts and humanities students fell by more than a third to 33,000, meaning that this area went from being the second most popular to the least popular of the five.

academicTask1.prompt: The pie charts below show the sources used to generate electricity on the island of Tarrin in 2000 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Electricity generation on Tarrin by source

keyFeatures: Fossil fuels produced 84% of the island's electricity in 2000 but only 41% in 2025, while renewables rose from 16% to 59%
Oil, the largest source in 2000 (44%), fell to 12%, and coal shrank from 23% to just 3%
Natural gas was the only fossil fuel to grow, from 17% to 26%
Wind became the largest single source (from 4% to 29%) and solar rose from 1% to 17%, whereas hydroelectric power changed little (11% to 13%)
academicTask1.model:
The two pie charts illustrate how the electricity produced on the island of Tarrin was generated in 2000 and 2025.

Overall, there was a marked shift away from fossil fuels towards renewable energy over the 25-year period. Wind power replaced oil as the leading source of electricity, and natural gas was the only fossil fuel to increase its share.

In 2000, fossil fuels dominated electricity generation, accounting for 84% of the total. Oil alone provided 44%, almost twice as much as coal (23%), while natural gas contributed 17%. Renewable sources were far less significant: hydroelectric plants supplied 11%, wind 4% and solar power just 1%.

By 2025, the combined share of fossil fuels had fallen to 41%. Oil dropped sharply to 12%, and coal dwindled to a mere 3%. Natural gas, in contrast, rose to 26%. The biggest gain was made by wind power, whose share rose more than sevenfold to 29%, making it the largest single source. Solar energy also expanded significantly to 17%, whereas the proportion from hydroelectric plants remained relatively stable at 13%.

academicTask1.prompt: The table below shows the number of visitors to five attractions in the city of Calderport in 2004, 2014 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Annual visitors to five attractions in Calderport (thousands)

keyFeatures: Over the whole period, attendance grew at every attraction except the Maritime Museum, and the combined total rose from about 1.34 million to almost 2.3 million
The castle was the most visited attraction in 2004 and 2014, but the Science Centre, which opened after 2004, overtook it in 2024 (655,000 against 640,000)
The Maritime Museum was the only attraction to decline steadily, from 380,000 to 210,000, dropping from second place to last
The Botanic Gardens almost doubled their visitors, while the Art Gallery peaked in 2014 (350,000) and then fell to 300,000
academicTask1.model:
The table compares the number of people who visited five tourist attractions in Calderport in three different years: 2004, 2014 and 2024.

Overall, the city's attractions became considerably more popular during this period, with the only consistent decline seen at the Maritime Museum. Another notable feature is that the Science Centre, which had not yet opened in 2004, had become the most visited attraction by the end of the period.

In 2004, the castle was the leading attraction, receiving 520,000 visitors, followed by the Maritime Museum with 380,000. The Botanic Gardens and the Art Gallery were less popular, attracting 245,000 and 190,000 visitors respectively. Over the next decade, the castle's figure rose to 610,000 and the Art Gallery's climbed sharply to 350,000, whereas the Maritime Museum's fell to 295,000. Meanwhile, the newly opened Science Centre attracted 410,000 people.

By 2024, the Science Centre had overtaken the castle, with 655,000 visitors compared with 640,000. The Botanic Gardens also became steadily more popular, reaching 480,000, almost double their 2004 total. In contrast, the Maritime Museum's figure dropped again to just 210,000, the lowest of all five sites that year, and the Art Gallery saw a modest fall to 300,000.

academicTask1.prompt: The diagram below shows how a sea stack is formed along a rocky coastline. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: How a sea stack is formed
steps: Waves strike a headland of hard rock that contains natural cracks and weak points
The force of the water, together with sand and pebbles hurled against the cliff, widens the cracks at its base
Over many years, the largest crack is eroded into a cave at sea level
The cave deepens until it breaks through the headland, creating a natural arch
Waves continue to erode the base of the arch, while rain, wind and frost weaken its roof
The roof collapses into the sea, leaving an isolated pillar of rock called a stack
The base of the stack is gradually undercut by the waves until the column topples
A low stump of rock remains, often visible only at low tide

keyFeatures: The process has eight stages and takes place over a very long period, beginning with cracks in a headland and ending with a low stump of rock
Wave erosion at the base of the rock is the main force at work throughout the process
The landforms appear in a fixed sequence: crack, cave, arch, stack and finally stump
Weathering by rain, wind and frost also weakens the roof of the arch until it collapses

academicTask1.prompt: The diagram below shows how wooden pencils are manufactured. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: The manufacture of wooden pencils
steps: Cedar logs are sawn into thin rectangular boards called slats
The slats are stained, waxed and dried in a kiln
Nine parallel grooves are cut along the surface of each slat
Meanwhile, powdered graphite and clay are mixed with water to make a thick paste
The paste is squeezed through a narrow nozzle to form thin rods, which are cut to length and baked at about 1,000°C to harden them
The hardened leads are laid in the grooves of one slat, and a second grooved slat is glued on top to form a 'sandwich'
The sandwiches are clamped and left to dry, then cut into nine separate pencils and shaped
Each pencil is painted with several coats of lacquer, stamped with the brand name and fitted with an eraser

keyFeatures: There are eight stages, with two separate strands (preparing the wooden slats and making the leads) that come together when the leads are fitted into the grooves
The wooden casing begins as cedar logs, which are sawn into slats, treated, kiln-dried and grooved
The leads are made from a paste of graphite, clay and water that is shaped into rods and baked at about 1,000°C
After assembly, the pencils are cut, shaped, lacquered, stamped and fitted with erasers
academicTask1.model:
The diagram illustrates how wooden pencils are manufactured, from cedar logs and graphite to the finished product.

Overall, the process consists of eight stages and involves two separate lines of work: preparing the wooden casing and making the leads. These come together when the leads are inserted into the wood, after which the pencils are cut, shaped and finished.

To begin with, cedar logs are sawn into thin rectangular boards known as slats. These are stained, waxed and kiln-dried, after which nine parallel grooves are cut into each one. Meanwhile, the leads are made separately. Powdered graphite and clay are combined with water to form a thick paste, which is forced through a narrow nozzle to create thin rods. These are cut to length and baked at around 1,000°C to harden them.

In the next stage, the leads are laid in the grooves of one slat and a second grooved slat is glued on top, forming a 'sandwich'. Once these have been clamped and dried, they are cut into nine individual pencils and shaped. Finally, each pencil is coated with several layers of lacquer, stamped with the brand name and fitted with an eraser.

academicTask1.prompt: The maps below show an area on the northern edge of the town of Maddleton in 2000 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Riverside area of Maddleton, 2000 and 2025 (north at top)

keyFeatures: Overall, the area changed from a largely rural and industrial landscape into a residential and commercial one, while the two main roads and the original houses stayed the same
North of Mill Road, the farmland was replaced by a housing estate and a park, and a shopping centre now stands on the site of the paper mill; the car park was kept
A bridge now carries Ash Lane across the river, and a riverside walk has been built along the southern bank
South of Mill Road, the school doubled in size and almost half of the woodland was cleared for a health centre
academicTask1.model:
The two maps illustrate how an area on the northern edge of Maddleton, beside the River Avel, changed between 2000 and 2025.

Overall, the district was transformed from a largely rural and industrial area into a residential and commercial one, with better transport links and new public facilities. However, the main roads and the existing houses remained the same.

In 2000, the western part of the land between the river and Mill Road was farmland, with a paper mill to the east of it and a car park on the far side of Ash Lane. By 2025, the farmland had made way for a housing estate and a small park, and the paper mill had been replaced by a shopping centre, while the car park was retained. In addition, a bridge had been built to carry Ash Lane across the river, and a riverside walk had been created along the southern bank, west of the bridge.

South of Mill Road, the houses were unaffected, but the school was extended southwards, roughly doubling in size. The most significant change on this side, however, was the clearance of almost half of the woodland to make room for a health centre.

generalTask1.prompt: You recently attended a weekend photography course run by a private company. Several things about the course were different from what was advertised. Write a letter to the company. In your letter
bullets: describe what the advertisement for the course promised
explain how the course was different
say what you would like the company to do
generalTask1.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to express my disappointment with the weekend photography course I attended at your Westgate studio on 14–15 September.

According to the advertisement on your website, the course was designed for beginners, with no more than eight participants, and included a full day of outdoor practice in the old harbour area. Lunch on both days was also promised, and the fee of £240 was said to cover all equipment.

Unfortunately, the reality was quite different. There were nineteen people in the group, so the tutor had very little time to look at our work. Moreover, the outdoor session was replaced by a two-hour slideshow, apparently because no permit had been arranged. We were also asked to pay an extra £35 to hire tripods, and lunch was provided on the Saturday only.

Given that the course fell so far short of its description, I would be grateful if you could refund half of the fee. Alternatively, I would accept a free place on a properly organised outdoor session in the near future.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,

Daniel Okoro

generalTask1.prompt: Your local council is planning to turn a small public garden near your home into a car park. Write a letter to the council. In your letter
bullets: explain how local people use the garden at present
describe the problems a car park would cause
suggest a better solution
generalTask1.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing in response to the council's proposal to replace Rowan Gardens on Mercer Street with a car park. As a resident of the street for over ten years, I would strongly urge you to reconsider.

Although the garden is small, it is in constant use. Parents from the nursery opposite take their children there to play, older residents meet on the benches every morning, and volunteers have recently planted a vegetable patch which supplies the local community kitchen.

Building a car park here would create several problems. Mercer Street is narrow and already congested, so extra traffic would make it more dangerous for the young children who cross it every day. Furthermore, removing the trees would increase noise and air pollution in a neighbourhood that has little green space.

I appreciate that parking is limited, but there is a better solution. The council could reach an agreement with the supermarket on Hale Road, whose large car park is half empty most evenings and at weekends, so that residents could use it.

Thank you for considering my views.

Yours faithfully,

Mei Lin Tan

I am writing to ask whether it would be possible to adjust my working hours for the next four months so that I can attend a part-time course.

The course, a Certificate in Data Analysis at Kesterton College, runs from October to January and covers spreadsheet modelling, data visualisation and basic programming. Classes take place on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons from 2 to 5 p.m.

I believe the qualification would be of real benefit to our team. At present, we rely on the finance department whenever we need sales figures analysed, which often delays our monthly reports. After completing the course, I would be able to prepare these analyses myself and pass on my new skills to colleagues.

To make up the time, I could start at 7.30 a.m. on those two days and leave at 1.30 p.m., and I would be happy to work later on Mondays and Wednesdays if necessary. I would make sure that none of my deadlines were affected.

task2.prompt: Some educators argue that secondary schools should set aside one full day each week for students to work on independent projects of their own choosing, instead of following the normal timetable. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

for: develops independence, research and time-management skills
lets students explore interests that the curriculum ignores
can renew motivation among students bored by routine lessons
against: a fifth of teaching time would be lost from core subjects
less organised students may waste the day without close guidance
projects are hard to assess fairly and need extra staff and resources

task2.model:
In most secondary schools, almost every hour of the week is devoted to a fixed curriculum, leaving students little opportunity to pursue their own interests. Some educators therefore propose that one day a week should be given over entirely to self-chosen projects. While I agree that independent project work deserves a place in the timetable, I believe that devoting a full day to it every week would be a mistake.

There are strong arguments for giving students more freedom. When teenagers choose a project themselves, whether it is building a simple app or researching the history of their neighbourhood, they tend to work with a level of commitment that routine lessons rarely inspire. Such projects also develop abilities that conventional classes often neglect, such as planning a task over several weeks, finding reliable information and presenting results to an audience.

However, a whole day each week represents a fifth of all teaching time. For students preparing for national examinations, losing this much instruction in mathematics, languages and science could seriously affect their results. Furthermore, independent work suits some learners far better than others. Highly motivated students may flourish, but those who struggle with organisation could easily drift through the day without making real progress, widening the gap between stronger and weaker students rather than narrowing it.

A more balanced approach would be to set aside a shorter period, perhaps one afternoon a week, for supervised projects with clear milestones and regular feedback from a teacher. This would preserve most of the benefits of independent study while protecting core subjects and ensuring that less confident students receive the support they need.

In conclusion, project-based learning has genuine value, but it should complement the curriculum rather than replace a significant part of it.

task2.prompt: In many countries, an increasing proportion of the population is over the age of 65. Some people think that the best way to care for older people is to help them live in their own homes for as long as possible, rather than moving them into care homes. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

for: older people keep their independence, routines and links with neighbours
home care is often cheaper for families and governments than residential care
familiar surroundings support mental well-being
against: people with serious illnesses may need round-the-clock professional care
living alone can lead to isolation and loneliness
adapting homes and arranging visits can place a heavy burden on relatives

task2.model:
As life expectancy rises, societies must decide how best to support their oldest members. Some people argue that older people should be helped to remain in their own homes for as long as possible rather than moving into care homes. I largely agree with this view, although I accept that for some individuals residential care is the safer and kinder option.

The strongest argument for supporting older people at home is that it allows them to keep control over their own lives. Someone who has lived in the same house for decades knows the neighbours, the local shops and the bus routes, and these familiar routines give structure and meaning to each day. Moving into an institution, however comfortable, often means giving up this independence. There is also a financial case: with simple adaptations such as handrails and stairlifts, and regular visits from carers, many people can live safely at home for considerably less than a care-home place costs.

Nevertheless, home care has clear limits. A person with advanced dementia or complex medical needs may require supervision day and night, which visiting carers cannot provide. In such cases, insisting on independence can expose the individual to real danger and place an exhausting burden on relatives. Loneliness is another serious risk, particularly for those who have lost a partner and rarely leave the house.

For these reasons, I believe that staying at home should be the starting point, backed by well-funded community services, but not an absolute rule. Each decision should be made on an individual basis, with the wishes of the older person at its centre.

In short, helping older people to remain in their own homes is generally the best approach, provided that good care homes remain available for those whose needs cannot be met in any other way.

task2.prompt: Some people believe that scientific research should focus mainly on solving practical problems, such as disease and climate change. Others argue that research driven purely by curiosity is just as important. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

for: urgent problems such as epidemics and food shortages need solutions now
taxpayers expect visible returns on public money
clear goals make funding easier to justify and progress easier to measure
against: many major breakthroughs began as research with no obvious use
nobody can predict which knowledge will prove useful
open-ended research attracts and trains talented scientists

task2.model:
Governments and universities have limited funds for research, so they must decide what kind of science to support. Some argue that the priority should be work that tackles pressing practical problems, while others maintain that research motivated simply by curiosity is equally valuable. In my view, both kinds of research are essential, and prioritising one at the expense of the other would be short-sighted.

Those who favour applied research point to the scale of the challenges facing the world. Diseases such as malaria still kill hundreds of thousands of people every year, and rising temperatures threaten harvests and coastal cities. When problems are this urgent, it seems reasonable to direct scientists towards finding solutions. Moreover, most research is funded by taxpayers, who are more likely to support such spending if they can see clear benefits, such as a new vaccine or a cheaper solar panel.

On the other hand, many of the most important practical advances have grown out of research that had no obvious use at the time. The physicists who first studied the strange behaviour of electrons in the early twentieth century could not have imagined that their work would one day make computers and smartphones possible. Since no one can predict which discoveries will prove useful, restricting funding to projects with immediate applications risks cutting off the source of future breakthroughs.

I believe the most sensible approach is to fund both. Applied research is clearly needed to address current crises, but a significant share of funding should still be reserved for open-ended investigation, because this is the foundation on which practical solutions are eventually built.

Ultimately, although it is understandable that people want science to deliver tangible results, curiosity-driven research is not a luxury but a long-term investment, and it deserves continued support alongside work on practical problems.

task2.prompt: Some people believe that parents should make important family decisions, such as moving to a new city or choosing a school, without involving their children. Others think that children should have a say in decisions of this kind. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

for: parents understand the full picture, such as finances and job prospects
children tend to focus on short-term wishes, such as staying near friends
protects children from adult worries and responsibility
against: children who are consulted feel respected and adapt better to change
children may know things parents miss, such as their real interests or problems at school
taking part in family discussions teaches decision-making skills

task2.model:
Choices such as moving to another city or selecting a secondary school can shape a child's life for years. Some people feel that such decisions are for parents alone, while others argue that children should be given a voice. In my view, children should be consulted, although the final responsibility must remain with their parents.

Those who favour leaving children out of these decisions make some valid points. Parents generally have a much fuller picture of the situation, including the family's finances and job prospects, whereas a ten-year-old is likely to focus on short-term concerns, such as staying close to friends. There is also an argument that children should be protected from adult worries. Asking a child to help decide whether the family can afford to move, for example, may cause unnecessary anxiety and place an unfair burden on them.

On the other hand, there are strong reasons for involving children. Young people who are asked for their opinion are more likely to feel respected, and they tend to adapt more easily to a change they have helped to shape. A teenager who has visited a new school and discussed it with their parents will probably start there with a more positive attitude than one who is simply told where to go. Children may also know things that their parents do not, such as which subjects they are passionate about or whether a particular school has a problem with bullying. Moreover, taking part in such discussions teaches them to weigh up options, a skill they will need as adults.

In conclusion, while parents should have the final say on major family matters, I believe that children's views deserve to be heard, and that they should carry more weight as children grow older. This approach respects young people's feelings without burdening them with responsibilities they are not yet ready to bear.

against: the lost fare income has to be replaced through taxes

some new passengers switch from walking or cycling rather than from cars

task2.model:
In an effort to reduce traffic and help residents with the cost of living, a number of cities have abolished fares on their buses and trams. Although this policy has some drawbacks, I believe that its benefits are greater, provided that it is properly funded.

The most obvious disadvantage is cost. Fares usually cover a substantial share of the expense of running a transport network, so when they disappear, the money has to be found elsewhere, typically through higher local taxes. Critics also point out that free travel can lead to overcrowding, as services designed for a certain number of paying passengers are suddenly used by many more. In addition, some of the new passengers may be people who previously walked or cycled, which does little to benefit the environment.

On the other hand, the advantages are considerable. Free public transport makes a real difference to people on low incomes, for whom travel costs can be a barrier to finding work, attending college or seeing a doctor. Cities also save the money they previously spent on ticket machines, inspectors and fare collection. Most importantly, when the policy is combined with measures such as dedicated bus lanes and higher parking charges, it can persuade drivers to leave their cars at home, which reduces congestion and improves air quality for everyone.

On balance, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but only if the city is prepared to invest in more frequent services and to discourage car use at the same time. A free network that is slow and overcrowded will not change people's habits, whereas one that is free, frequent and reliable can transform the way a city moves.

task2.prompt: Large quantities of clothing are thrown away every year, often after being worn only a few times. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to reduce it?

for: cheap, fast-changing fashion encourages frequent buying
social media pressure not to be seen in the same outfit twice
low-quality garments wear out quickly and are rarely repaired
against: making manufacturers pay for collecting and recycling their products
promoting repair, clothes swaps and second-hand shops
labels showing how long a garment is designed to last

task2.model:
In many parts of the world, clothes are bought, worn a handful of times and then thrown away, creating vast quantities of textile waste. This problem has both economic and social causes, but there are practical steps that could reduce it.

The principal cause is the rise of so-called fast fashion. Large retailers now release new collections every few weeks, and garments are so cheap that a new top can cost less than a sandwich and a coffee. When clothes are this inexpensive, people come to see them as disposable. Social media has intensified the problem, since many young people feel under pressure not to be photographed in the same outfit twice. Finally, much of this clothing is poorly made, so seams split and colours fade after a few washes, and few people have the skills or the inclination to mend it.

Tackling the problem requires action from both governments and consumers. Governments could make manufacturers financially responsible for their products at the end of their life, for instance by requiring them to fund collection and recycling schemes. This would give companies a strong incentive to design clothes that last longer and are easier to recycle. At the same time, campaigns in schools and the media could promote alternatives to buying new, such as clothes-swapping events, second-hand shops and basic sewing skills. Labels showing how many washes a garment is designed to withstand might also help shoppers make better-informed choices.

To sum up, the throwaway culture surrounding clothing is driven largely by low prices, social pressure and poor quality. Holding producers responsible for waste, while encouraging consumers to repair, share and reuse, offers the most realistic way of reducing it.

task2.prompt: Many people now get most of their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. Why is this the case? How might it affect the way people understand current events?

for: news on social media is free, instant and on the phone people already carry
feeds are personalised and use short, engaging formats such as video clips
people trust stories shared by friends and like to comment on them
against: algorithms mainly show people views they already agree with
false or misleading stories spread widely before they are corrected
short posts leave out context, encouraging a shallow understanding

task2.model:
Over the past decade, social media platforms have overtaken newspapers and television as the main source of news for many people, especially the young. There are several clear reasons for this shift, and in my view its effects on public understanding of current events are more harmful than helpful.

The most obvious explanation is convenience. Most people now carry a smartphone at all times, and social media apps deliver news instantly and free of charge, whereas newspapers increasingly require a subscription and television bulletins are broadcast at fixed times. In addition, news on these platforms comes in short, eye-catching formats, such as videos lasting less than a minute, which suit people who are busy or easily distracted. Finally, many users trust stories shared by friends more than those presented by traditional media organisations, which they may regard as distant or biased.

However, this change has worrying consequences. Because platforms use algorithms that show users more of what they have already clicked on, people tend to see mainly views they already agree with, and they may come to believe that their opinions are more widely held than they really are. False or exaggerated stories can also reach millions of people within hours, long before any correction appears. Moreover, a thirty-second clip rarely provides the background needed to understand complex issues such as an economic crisis or a war, so audiences may form strong opinions on the basis of very little information.

To conclude, people have turned to social media for news mainly because it is fast, free and personal. Unfortunately, these same qualities can leave them with a narrower and less accurate picture of the world, which is why teaching people to question what they see online has become so important.

task2.prompt: Computer programs are increasingly being used to make decisions that were previously made by people, such as who should receive a bank loan or be invited to a job interview. Is this a positive or negative development?

for: decisions are faster and cheaper to make

against: programs can repeat biases hidden in past data

task2.model:
Banks, employers and even public agencies now rely on software to make choices that were once made by trained staff, such as approving a loan or shortlisting job applicants. While this offers some clear benefits, I believe that, in its current form, the trend is more negative than positive.

Supporters of automated decision-making emphasise its efficiency. A program can assess thousands of applications in the time it would take a person to read a few, which reduces costs and shortens waiting times. It is also argued that software is fairer, because it applies the same criteria to every applicant and is not influenced by tiredness, mood or personal prejudice.

However, the claim that such programs are neutral is often mistaken. Most of them learn from historical data, so if past decisions were biased against certain groups, such as women or people from particular neighbourhoods, the software is likely to reproduce that bias on a far larger scale. A further problem is transparency. When a human rejects an application, the applicant can usually ask for an explanation, but automated systems are frequently unable to justify their conclusions in terms that ordinary people can understand. As a result, individuals may be refused a job interview or a mortgage without knowing why or how to appeal.

For these reasons, I consider the growing reliance on automated decisions to be a largely negative development at present. It could become a positive one if organisations were legally required to explain their decisions and to allow a human to review any outcome that is challenged. Until such safeguards are widespread, however, the risks to fairness outweigh the gains in speed and cost.
